https://hjkellis.github.io/cart-pole/.body:
This is my solution to the classic Cart-Pole problem, using a simple PID controller implemented in python and Gymnasium.
Proportional-Derivative Control
For balancing the pole a simple PD controller was sufficient. In my implementation, I approximated the derivative error with a Tustin transform.
PD Controller:
$$u(t)=K_p\cdot e(t)+K_d\cdot\frac{de(t)}{dt}$$
discrete approximation,
$$\Rightarrow u[n]\approx K_p\cdot e[n]+2K_d\cdot\frac{e[n]-e[n-1]}{T_s}$$
Integral Control
For integral control, I used a backwards euler approximation - where $K_i\int^{t}_{0}{e(\tau)d\tau}$ is the integral term:
$$K_i\int^{t}_{0}{e(\tau)d\tau}\approx K_i T_s\sum^{n}_{k=1}{e[k]}$$
To deal with memory constraints, a ring buffer was used to capture the integral over a fixed range.
Code
Here is the very simple code snippet of my controller logic. $T_s$ and other constants are aggregated into the controller gains and prev_errs is a ring buffer.
Result
This simple application of PID yields a decently stable output, but I still need to do some parameter tuning especially on the integral term.

https://hjkellis.github.io/posts/scylla-.body:
3D-Printed and handwired a Bastard Keyboards' Scylla.
Here is a list of materials I used:
58 $\times$ 1N4148 Flyback Diodes
58 $\times$ Gateron Brown Switches
2 $\times$ Pro Micro Dev Boards
2 $\times$ Female Aux Connectors
2 $\times$ Female Aux Connectors
3D Printer Filament
3D Printed Case
The print took ~12 hours total (6 hours for each side) on a BambuLabs A1 mini.
3D printed case, still on the print-plate.
Wiring
I hand soldered each board, this ended being the most laborious part of this project as each side of the keyboard has 29 keys. Additionally, with 3 solder joints (2 wires and a diode) per key, 30 connections to the microcontroller, and 3 connections to the AUX jack, this worked out to $2 \times 29 + 2 \times 5 \times 6 + 2 \times 6 = 124$ solder joints in total. I also had to cut and strip each wire to fit properly into the case.
Keyboard wiring (minus the μC)
Firmware & Keymaps
For the firmware I used QMK, an "open-source keyboard firmware for Atmel AVR and Arm USB families". I had to write my own hardware configuration files to match with my microcontroller and wiring. The documentation for QMK and made things super easy.
For keymaps I have 4 layers, one for typing, the second and third for symbols, arrow keys, and function keys, and the last is a special layer that is triggered when both layer keys are pressed that accesses some system features.
All layers have a transparent thumb cluster.
Base Layer
For my base layer I am just using a standard QWERTY.
Upper Layer
The upper layer contains symbols and function keys
Lower Layer
The lower layer just contains arrow keys.
System Layer
Finally, there is a final layer that is triggered when both layer keys are pressed simultaniously that allows me to control the mouse and other system features.
Finished Product
This is the final product with keycaps installed!
Finished product

https://hjkellis.github.io/projects/mirr.body:
I modified a Lululemon workout mirror so that I could use a Raspberry Pi to display a custom dashboard through the mirrors display.
Hardware
Lululemon stopped producing these mirrors and they require users to pay for a subscription to use the mirror for its intended purpose. As a result I was able to snag one of these second had for \$150 (they originally sold for \$1500!). The hardware on these mirrors is great, especially compared to many of the DIY smart mirrors floating around the internet.
Internals of the Mirror(it is just a LCD and a two way mirror)
I only made slight modifcations to the internals of the mirror to get it to work how I wanted, this included replacing the display driver and SBC that came with the mirror with a matching display driver I found on ebay and a Raspberry Pi 3 - Model B that I had sitting around since highschool. After that it was just a matter of some cable management to route power to the RPI and the hardware was all finished.
RPI Desktop Displayed on Mirror
From there I accesssed the Pi via SSH and had my way with this machine.
Software
Github Repo
Mirror displaying weather and time.

https://hjkellis.github.io/projects/robo.body:
Intro
This project article documents building of a 6-DOF robotic arm (modified version of an open-source hardware design by tw2ka with custom electronics and firmware). Additionally, the hardware files, software packages, and firmware for this project can be found here.
Arm and Joint State Publisher
Hardware
The goal for the hardware side of this project was to reduce price while maintaining as much of the performance of the original design as possible. In order to accomplish this goal, hardware was constrained to consumer/hobbiest level electronics and 3D printed rigid bodies. Most of the control hardware was taken from an old 3D-printer I built in high school, for which I wrote custom firmware to integrate motor controls, serial communication, and position feedback.
Mechanical
The robotic arm consists of stepper motors, belts, pulleys, and 3D-printed rigid bodies. The first 5 joints (J1 to J5) use bipolar NEMA 17 stepper motors, while the last joint (J6), responsible for rotating the end effector, uses a bipolar NEMA 8 stepper motor. All belts are off-the-shelf GT2 timing belts. Ball and shunt bearings were also used in various sizes to reduce friction between joints.
Stepper motors with feedback sensors
Electrical
A recycled RAMPS stepper motor board was used to control the stepper motors, with micro-stepping applied for higher resolution. A neodymium magnet was attached to the back of each stepper motor shaft with a AS5600 magnetic encoder to read joint positions. Finally, communication with the ROS2 control package was established via UART over USB.
RAMPS control board.
Encoder feedback was mostly used to for backdriving the robotic arm. But a simple closed loop control scheme was also added to ensure accurate postion tracking.
Postion feedback system
Closed-loop control of the stepper motors was managed by the custom RAMPS firmware and a simple proportional feedback controller. Luckily, the mechanical design led the steppers to rarely lose steps.
Software
The ROS2 packages for this project can be found here.
Kinematic chain visualization (RViz)

https://hjkellis.github.io/projects/rock.body:
In this project I design a LQI (Linear Quadratic Integral) controller in MATLAB to simulate the landing of a rocket. This was my final project for one of my graduate school courses Applied Linear Systems.
From non-linear ODEs describing the rockets dynamics -- I linearized the model and designed an appropriate LQI controller to safely land the rocket in the simulation.
Linearized rocket equations:
$$M\ddot{y}(t)=F_{ss}+f(t)-\alpha\dot{y}(t)-Mg$$
$$J\ddot{\theta}(t)=T_{ss}+\tau(t)-\beta\dot{\theta}(t)$$
$$M\ddot{x}(t)=-F_{ss}\theta(t)-\gamma\dot{x}(t)$$
LQI controllers are an type of optimal control that is similar to LQR (Linear Quadratic Regulator) controllers. In essence LQI is just LQR with the addition of a integral term. This integral term allows for better point tracking.
Here are the results:
Landing the rocket at the origin.
Landing the rocket in chopsticks, based on a simple flight trajectory.
